options.metric: Annual percentage of eligible crashes with at least one person injured or killed, calculated as 100 times crashes with number_of_persons_injured + number_of_persons_killed > 0 divided by eligible crash rows.
options.denominator: Count of eligible police-reported crash rows in each year and time group; eligible means crash_time and both person outcome counts are nonmissing. Midnight rows are a separate group, and the night/day comparison uses the remaining clock times.
options.grouping: Calendar year and three clock-time groups: night 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59; day 06:00–19:59; exactly 00:00:00 is reported separately as midnight/possible default.
options.chart_type: Annual line chart with separate day, night, and midnight/possible-default series.
options.reason: A crash-level injury-or-death share directly describes how often a reported crash in each clock-time group involved recorded human harm.
options.answer: The dataset can answer only partly: the injury-or-death crash share was higher at night in 2013 (23.77% vs 18.63% by day), while in 2025 the daytime share was higher (44.29% vs 42.41% at night).
options.interpretation: Only partly: for complete years 2013–2025, this chart reports the annual share of eligible police-reported crashes with at least one recorded injury or death, calculated as injury-or-death crashes divided by eligible crash rows; night means 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59, day means 06:00–19:59, and 00:00 is shown separately as midnight/possible default. Night's share was higher through 2021 (36.64% vs 34.52% in 2021), while daytime's share was slightly higher in 2022 and reached 44.29% versus 42.41% at night in 2025. This is a defensible crash-level measure of injury involvement, but it does not measure risk per trip or actual darkness and cannot establish that darkness caused crashes. The check found 42 of 2,132,218 complete-year rows (0.001970%) missing at least one outcome count and excluded them (18 rows lacked the injured count and 36 lacked the killed count, with overlap); partial 2012 (100,545 rows) and 2026 (36,424 rows) were excluded, while 23,786 eligible 00:00 rows were separated after midnight records jumped from 24 in 2015 to 2,895 in 2016; the largest neighboring-year group-denominator change was 79,435 fewer day crashes from 2019 to 2020, so a rise or fall in the measure across those years may result from this denominator change rather than a change in the outcome and should be compared cautiously.

options.metric: Annual sum of number_of_persons_injured plus number_of_persons_killed per 100 eligible crashes.
options.denominator: Count of eligible police-reported crash rows in each year and time group; eligible means crash_time and both person outcome counts are nonmissing. Midnight rows are a separate group, and the night/day comparison uses the remaining clock times.
options.grouping: Calendar year and three clock-time groups: night 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59; day 06:00–19:59; exactly 00:00:00 is reported separately as midnight/possible default.
options.chart_type: Annual line chart with separate day, night, and midnight/possible-default series.
options.reason: A casualty-per-crash rate captures both whether harm occurred and the number of injured or killed people in each reported crash.
options.answer: The dataset can answer only partly: recorded injured-plus-killed people per 100 crashes were higher at night than by day in every complete year, including 60.18 versus 57.57 in 2025.
options.interpretation: Only partly: for complete years 2013–2025, this chart reports the annual sum of recorded injured plus killed people divided by eligible police-reported crash rows and multiplied by 100; night means 20:00–23:59 and 00:01–05:59, day means 06:00–19:59, and 00:00 is shown separately as midnight/possible default. The nighttime casualty burden per 100 crashes exceeded daytime in each complete year, including 60.18 versus 57.57 in 2025. This is a defensible measure of recorded casualty burden per reported crash, but it is not a per-trip danger rate, does not account for traffic exposure or actual darkness, and cannot establish causation. The check found 42 of 2,132,218 complete-year rows (0.001970%) missing at least one outcome count and excluded them (18 rows lacked the injured count and 36 lacked the killed count, with overlap); partial 2012 (100,545 rows) and 2026 (36,424 rows) were excluded, while 23,786 eligible 00:00 rows were separated after midnight records jumped from 24 in 2015 to 2,895 in 2016; the largest neighboring-year group-denominator change was 79,435 fewer day crashes from 2019 to 2020, so a rise or fall in the measure across those years may result from this denominator change rather than a change in the outcome and should be compared cautiously.
